turkic_kayra.name: Divide the cosmos into the three realms of air, water and land
turkic_kayra.notes: From the primordial waters the creator-father structures the layered cosmos — the heavens above, the earth, and the underworld below — separating the realms of good and evil before begetting the ordering gods.

sources.reference: Jean-Paul Roux, La religion des Turcs et des Mongols; Altai cosmogonic recitations (Radloff, Proben)

turkic_od.name: Purify and ward off evil through flame
turkic_od.notes: The hearth-fire personified as Ot/Od cleanses persons, dwellings and possessions; people and goods were passed by or around fire to drive off sickness and malign spirits.

sources.reference: Jean-Paul Roux, La religion des Turcs et des Mongols (the cult of fire, ot)

turkic_tengri.name: Create and order the heavens and the earth
turkic_tengri.notes: In the opening of the Orkhon (Kül Tigin / Bilge Khagan) inscriptions the blue sky above and the brown earth below are made, and humankind set between them, by Tengri's ordinance.

sources.reference: Orkhon inscriptions, Kül Tigin stele (east face, opening)

turkic_umay.name: Open the womb and bestow children
turkic_umay.notes: As mother-goddess of birth Umay grants offspring and presides over conception and safe delivery; her name is the Old Turkic word for the placenta/afterbirth, and khagan-consorts (katun) were likened to her.

sources.reference: Orkhon inscriptions (the simile 'umay teg ögüm katun', my mother the katun like the goddess Umay), Kül Tigin stele

udmurt_inmar.name: Send light, rain and benign weather from on high
udmurt_inmar.notes: As high sky-god of the aerial tier Inmar dispenses light and life-giving rain; white animals were immolated to him and prayers offered beneath the pine.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology

udmurt_kyldysin.name: Enrich the soil and grant the harvest
udmurt_kyldysin.notes: Earth-and-fertility god (the mu- 'earth' aspect Mu-Kylchin) who quickens the ploughland and crops; nineteenth-century records describe collective seasonal sacrifices seeking his blessing on soil and yield.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology

udmurt_nyulesmurt.name: Allot the game and decide each beast's lair
udmurt_nyulesmurt.notes: The forest-master apportions hunting and herding luck and is said to decide where each bear shall lie in its den; he can match his stature to the place — level with the trees in the wood, with the grass in the meadow.

sources.reference: Aado Lintrop, 'Forest Spirits in the Udmurt Worldview', Sator 22 (2021)

udmurt_vumurt.name: Grant or withhold the fish-catch and drown the heedless
udmurt_vumurt.notes: The water-man (vukuzyo, 'master of water') gives a rich catch when honoured but, offended, withholds the fish or even drags a lake to a new place; he drowns those who trespass on his waters and is blamed for accidents at mills and fords.

sources.reference: Aado Lintrop, 'On the Udmurt Water Spirit', Folklore (Tartu)

vainakh_sela_sata.name: Shine in countenance like the sun
vainakh_sela_sata.notes: The crafts-goddess, counterpart of the Northwest-Caucasian Satanaya, is described as having a face that shines with the beauty of the sun.

sources.reference: John Colarusso, Nart Sagas from the Caucasus; Vainakh-religion survey

wabanaki_gluskap.name: Give the people fire, tobacco, nets and canoes
wabanaki_gluskap.notes: As culture-hero Gluskap brings the Wabanaki their useful arts — fire, tobacco, fishing nets, earthenware and the canoe — and the knowledge of good and evil.

sources.reference: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884); Silas T. Rand, Legends of the Micmacs (1894)

vanuatu_qat.name: Buy night and cut the first dawn
vanuatu_qat.notes: Finding the world in perpetual day, Qat sails to Vava (the Torres Islands) to buy Night from I-Qong; he teaches the people sleep, then cuts the dawn with a red obsidian knife so that day and night should alternate.

sources.reference: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians (1891), ch. on Qat
Mircea Eliade, Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy (the Altai horse-sacrifice and ascent to Bai Ülgen)

udmurt_vumurt.name: His comb (left at the waterside; not to be taken)

sources.reference: 'Water Bodies in Besserman tradition', Sator 22 (2021); Aado Lintrop, 'On the Udmurt Water Spirit'

vainakh_pkharmat.name: The sheedag (reed-pipe shaped during his torment)

sources.reference: Amjad Jaimoukha, The Chechens: A Handbook (Pkharmat / Nart cycle)
Vainakh-religion survey; John Colarusso, Nart Sagas from the Caucasus

vanuatu_marawa.name: His spider's web (binds and finishes Qat's canoe)

sources.reference: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians (1891), ch. on Qat

vietnamese_tan_vien_son_thanh.name: Magic staff and divine book of arts

sources.reference: Lĩnh Nam chích quái (Wonders Plucked from the Dust of Linh-nam), tale of Tản Viên / Sơn Tinh

vietnamese_thanh_giong.name: Uprooted bamboo clumps wielded as weapons

sources.reference: Lĩnh Nam chích quái, legend of Phù Đổng Thiên Vương (Thánh Gióng)

sources.reference: Bilge Khagan inscription (opening titulature)

Amjad Jaimoukha, The Chechens: A Handbook (Nart cycle)

vietnamese_lieu_hanh.rom: Quỳnh Hoa Liễu Hạnh công chúa

sources.reference: Scripture of the Four Palaces (Tứ Phủ)
Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (Hồng Bàng annals); cult at Đền Mẫu Âu Cơ, Phú Thọ

vainakh_tusholi.gloss: goddess of spring and fertility, the people's intercessor with Däl

sources.reference: Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes
R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians (1891)

turkic_tengri.name: Heaven-sacrifice on the mountain heights
turkic_tengri.cadence: seasonal / at need by the khagan
turkic_tengri.notes: The steppe peoples sacrificed horses and cattle to Heaven on high places; the Shiji records the Xiongnu offering to tian (Tengri) on mountain-tops, and worship was made by raising the hands and bowing toward the sky.

sources.reference: Sima Qian, Shiji 110 (Xiongnu chapter)

turkic_ulgen.name: The white horse-sacrifice and shaman's ascent
turkic_ulgen.notes: An Altai kam set up a yurt enclosing a young birch notched with steps (tapty); a white horse was sacrificed and the shaman, mounting its soul, climbed the heavens stage by stage to lay the offering before Bai Ülgen.

sources.reference: Wilhelm Radloff, Aus Sibirien; Mircea Eliade, Shamanism

turkic_od.name: Bridal circling of the hearth-fire
turkic_od.notes: A bride entering the household was led around the family hearth to honour the fire-mother (Ot/Od); the domestic flame was kept pure and never defiled, and fire was used to cleanse.

sources.reference: Jean-Paul Roux, La religion des Turcs et des Mongols (the cult of fire)

udmurt_inmar.name: White-animal sacrifice in the sacred grove
udmurt_inmar.notes: White animals were immolated to Inmar (black to Kyldysin, red to Kuaz); prayers led by the vösyas' priest were said under a pine in the sacred grove, the participants robed in white.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology; Aado Lintrop, Udmurt prayer-feast studies

udmurt_keremet.name: Black-animal propitiation in the keremet grove
udmurt_keremet.notes: In a secluded forest clearing (the keremet or lud) a special tuno priest sacrificed black animals to avert the misfortunes that the just but stern Lud sent on transgressors.

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology; 'Eastern Udmurt Sacred Places', Journal of Ethnology and Folkloristics

udmurt_vumurt.name: Riverside offering for the catch and the cattle
udmurt_vumurt.cadence: at the opening/close of fishing and at watering
udmurt_vumurt.notes: Fishermen and herders propitiated the water-master so the catch would be good and grazing cattle not drown; combs, soap or other objects found by the water were left untouched as his property.

sources.reference: 'Water Bodies in Besserman tradition', Sator 22 (2021); Aado Lintrop, 'On the Udmurt Water Spirit'

urartian_haldi.name: State sacrifice prescribed in the Meher Kapısı god-list
urartian_haldi.notes: On the Meher Kapısı rock inscription Haldi heads the pantheon with the largest allotment (bulls and sheep prescribed for him); even his attributes — his armies, spear, weapons and gates — receive their own offerings. His chief temple stood at Muṣaṣir/Ardini.

sources.reference: Meher Kapısı (Mheri Dur) inscription of Išpuini and Minua

urartian_teisheba.name: Temple worship at Teišebaini
urartian_teisheba.notes: The fortress-city Teišebaini (Karmir-Blur), founded by Rusa II, was named for and dedicated to the storm-god; he received temples and sacrifices alongside Haldi and Šivini.

sources.reference: Meher Kapısı inscription; Karmir-Blur (Teišebaini) excavation finds

urartian_bagmashtu.name: Votive cult as Haldi's consort at Muṣaṣir
urartian_bagmashtu.notes: In the eastern region around Muṣaṣir/Ardini votive objects name 'Haldi and his wife Bagmashtu (Bagbartu)'; her temple there was plundered by Sargon II of Assyria in 714 BCE.

sources.reference: Muṣaṣir votive inscriptions; Sargon II, Letter to the God Assur (eighth campaign, 714 BCE)

vainakh_tusholi.name: Spring Festival of Tusholi
vainakh_tusholi.cadence: annually in spring (April), at the hoopoe's return
vainakh_tusholi.notes: Timed to the return of the hoopoe ('Tusholi's hen', held sacred), the festival was led by a pure-man priest (tsyeni stag); pilgrims kissed the ground before her wooden idol with its iron mask, and childless women touched the image to seek offspring. Her sanctuary lay in the Assa gorge of Ingushetia.

sources.reference: Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes

vainakh_seela.name: Rain-and-harvest prayers in the month of Seli
vainakh_seela.cadence: in the spring month named for him (Seli-butt)
vainakh_seela.notes: In the month/moon bearing his name Sela was invoked for rain and a good harvest; those struck by his lightning were reckoned blessed and specially buried.

sources.reference: Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes

vainakh_maetsill.name: Harvest festival of Maetsill
vainakh_maetsill.notes: A harvest feast was kept in honour of the grain-god, who fills the fields and barns and protects the poor; his name is linked to the mountain sanctuary of Mat-Lam.

sources.reference: Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes; Vainakh-religion survey

vainakh_molyz_yerdy.name: Warriors' offerings at the sanctuary of Molyz-Yerdy
vainakh_molyz_yerdy.notes: Vainakh warriors made offerings at the war-god's shrine (yerdy/elgyts) to win victory and to give thanks for it.

sources.reference: Amjad Jaimoukha, The Chechens: A Handbook; Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes

vietnamese_tan_vien_son_thanh.name: Cult of Tản Viên Sơn Thánh (Và Temple, Ba Vì)
vietnamese_tan_vien_son_thanh.notes: Foremost of the Tứ Bất Tử (Four Immortals), the mountain-god of Ba Vì is honoured at scores of relics in the Hanoi region (notably the Và Temple in Sơn Tây), petitioned for good harvests and protection from flood and disaster.

sources.reference: Lĩnh Nam chích quái; Tản Viên Sơn Thánh festival inventory (Ba Vì), recognised national intangible heritage

vietnamese_thanh_giong.name: Gióng Festival of Phù Đổng and Sóc temples
vietnamese_thanh_giong.cadence: annually before the harvest (4th lunar month at Phù Đổng)
vietnamese_thanh_giong.notes: Re-enacts the hero's battle with a white horse and a flag-dance; he is venerated as patron of the harvest, national peace and family prosperity. Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage (2010).

sources.reference: UNESCO Representative List, 'Gióng festival of Phù Đổng and Sóc temples' (2010)

vietnamese_lieu_hanh.name: Phủ Giầy Festival of the Mother Goddess
vietnamese_lieu_hanh.cadence: annually, 3rd–10th day of the 3rd lunar month
vietnamese_lieu_hanh.notes: Centred on her temple complex at Phủ Giầy (Vụ Bản, Nam Định) with its Vân Cát and Tiên Hương palaces; marks the goddess's death anniversary with processions, offerings and hầu đồng spirit-mediumship. Đạo Mẫu was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016.

sources.reference: UNESCO, 'Practices related to the Viet beliefs in the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms' (2016); Phủ Giầy festival tradition

vietnamese_lac_long_quan.name: Ancestral cult at the Hùng Temples
vietnamese_lac_long_quan.cadence: ongoing; Hùng Kings' commemoration (10th day, 3rd lunar month)
vietnamese_lac_long_quan.notes: As progenitor of the Bách Việt with Âu Cơ, Lạc Long Quân is venerated with the Holy Ancestor and the Hùng kings at the Hùng Temple complex in Phú Thọ, where the temple keepers offer incense.

sources.reference: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (Hồng Bàng annals); Hùng Temple cult, Phú Thọ

vietnamese_au_co.name: Mother-of-the-Nation cult at Đền Mẫu Âu Cơ
vietnamese_au_co.notes: Venerated as Quốc Mẫu ('Mother of the Nation'), notably at Đền Mẫu Âu Cơ in Hiền Lương, Phú Thọ.

sources.reference: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư; cult at Đền Mẫu Âu Cơ, Phú Thọ

wabanaki_pamola.name: Taboo of the sacred summit of Katahdin
wabanaki_pamola.notes: Fear of Pamola, who brews storms and seizes climbers, made the summit of Mount Katahdin taboo; Penobscot guides refused to ascend, as Thoreau recorded in 1846 ('Pamola is always angry with those who climb to the summit of K'taadn').

sources.reference: Henry D. Thoreau, The Maine Woods (1864), 'Ktaadn'

attributes.name: The white waterfowl over the primal waters
attributes.notes: In Altai cosmogony the creator is figured neither as man nor woman but as a pure-white bird (goose/duck) flying ceaselessly over the boundless primordial sea before the making of the world.

sources.reference: Wilhelm Radloff, Proben der Volkslitteratur der türkischen Stämme; Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology

attributes.name: Aniconic — the eternal blue sky itself
attributes.notes: Kök Tengri is never figured in human or animal form; he is the blue heaven, with the sun and moon under his governance as his visible signs.

sources.reference: Jean-Paul Roux, La religion des Turcs et des Mongols
Sima Qian, Shiji 110; cf. Old Turkic kök at

attributes.name: Three-horned / three-pointed headdress
attributes.notes: Umay is figured with a distinctive triple-pointed headgear; the 'elibelinde' (hands-on-hips) mother-goddess motif of Anatolian kilims — a triangular female form with hooked arms — is taken to continue her ancient image.

sources.reference: Emel Esin, Türk Kozmolojisine Giriş; studies of the Anatolian 'elibelinde' kilim motif

sacredAnimals.name: Bird (the descending soul of the child)

sources.reference: Jean-Paul Roux, Faune et flore sacrées

sacredPlants.name: Birch (the cosmic tree / world-axis to his heaven)

sources.reference: Uno Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology; Eliade, Shamanism
Wilhelm Radloff, Aus Sibirien

attributes.name: Born with miraculous, partly bestial features and radiance
attributes.notes: The Oghuznāme describes the infant Oghuz with an awesome appearance — blue-grey of face, with features of ox, wolf, sable and bear — who matured and spoke within forty days.

sources.reference: Oghuznāme (Uyghur-script Oghuz Khagan epic)

sacredAnimals.name: The heaven-sent grey wolf (Boz Kurt), army-guide

sources.reference: Oghuznāme (Oghuz Khagan epic)

attributes.name: Warrior standing upon a lion, bearing a spear
attributes.notes: Haldi is portrayed as an armed man, with or without wings, standing on a lion; his temple at Muṣaṣir (shown on Sargon II's relief) carried a spear-finial on its gable with shields hung on the walls — 'the house of weapons'.

sources.reference: Relief of the sack of Muṣaṣir, palace of Sargon II at Khorsabad (714 BCE)
Khorsabad Muṣaṣir relief; Urartian bronze plaques

attributes.name: Standing on a bull, grasping thunderbolts, in a horned tiara
attributes.notes: The storm-god is figured as a man upon a bull holding a fistful of thunderbolts and wearing a tall horned headgear; the bronze statuette from Teišebaini (Karmir-Blur, found 1941) is the type-piece.

sources.reference: Bronze statuette of Teisheba from Teišebaini (Karmir-Blur)
Karmir-Blur (Teišebaini) finds

attributes.name: Long-haired youth kneeling on one knee, upholding the solar disc
attributes.notes: Šivini is shown as a young man with long hair, kneeling on one knee and raising a winged sun-disc above his head; the winged solar disc and the (winged) shield are his emblems.

sources.reference: studies of Urartian art, 'The Iconography and Symbolism of the Sun God in Urartian Art'

attributes.name: Chained to the summit of Bashlam (Kazbek), liver torn by the bird Ida
attributes.notes: After stealing Sela's fire on the swift horse Turpal, Pkharmat is chained by the cyclops Uja to Mount Bashlam/Kazbek, where the falcon Ida (king of birds) descends each dawn to devour his ever-regenerating liver — the Vainakh Prometheus.

sources.reference: Amjad Jaimoukha, The Chechens: A Handbook (Nart cycle)

attributes.name: Armed with the rainbow as a bow and lightning as arrows
attributes.notes: The touchy weather-god wields the rainbow ('Bow of Seela') as his bow and lightning-bolts as arrows, sending snow and hail from his seat on Mount Kazbek; the Milky Way is the 'scattering of Sela' and the Bow of Seela is the rainbow.

sources.reference: Mariel Tsaroïeva, Anciennes croyances des Ingouches et des Tchétchènes; Vainakh-religion survey

attributes.name: His great stone canoe
attributes.notes: Gluskap is associated with an immense stone canoe in which he withdraws to the world's edge, promising to return.

sources.reference: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884)

attributes.name: Transformer who became a giant beaver
attributes.notes: In a widely told tale he turns himself into a giant beaver and, slapping his tail, raises islands in the Bay of Fundy; as transformer he shapes the land and tames the monsters of the first age.

sources.reference: Silas T. Rand, Legends of the Micmacs (1894)

attributes.name: The wolf (his name means 'wolf' in Wabanaki)
attributes.notes: Malsumis ('Wolf the younger') is the evil twin who burst from his mother's side; he can be killed only by a blow from a fern-root, with which Gluskap at last slays him.

sources.reference: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of Glooskap's Birth and of his Brother Malsum the Wolf'

attributes.name: Moose-headed, man-bodied, eagle-winged and -taloned
attributes.notes: Pamola is described with the head of a moose, the body of a man and the wings and feet (talons) of an eagle; he embodies the cold storms of Katahdin.

sources.reference: Fannie Hardy Eckstorm, The Katahdin Legends; Penobscot tradition

attributes.name: Knife of red obsidian (cuts the first dawn)
attributes.notes: Qat carves the first people from dracaena wood and, having bought Night, cuts the dawn with a knife of red volcanic glass; with the spider Marawa he builds the first unsinkable canoe.

sources.reference: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians (1891), ch. on Qat
